title: Learning Robot Policies
blurb: Tests the three routes to a robot policy, reinforcement learning and reward design, behaviour cloning and distribution shift, DAgger, fine-tuning a pretrained VLA, how to choose, and why the cloned policy failed completely beside the obstacle.

refLinks.label: §63.2.3 Route 3: Fine-Tuning a Pretrained VLA Policy

questions.prompt: What does reinforcement learning need that behaviour cloning doesn't?
options: Expert demonstrations covering many states
A pretrained vision-language model
A scripted expert that can be queried
A reward signal and many episodes
questions.explanation: RL discovers behaviour by exploration against a reward, which takes many episodes, hence parallel simulators. Demonstrations and queryable experts belong to imitation learning.

questions.prompt: A legged robot rewarded for forward velocity learns to fall forward over and over. What is this?
options: Reward hacking
Representation collapse
The sim-to-real gap
Distribution shift
questions.explanation: The policy maximises the reward as written, not the intended behaviour. Falling forward scored more velocity than walking.

questions.prompt: Reward only on reaching the goal gives almost no learning signal early on. What does Procedure 63.1 suggest?
options: Remove the completion bonus and reward only smoothness.
Increase the network size until it learns.
Add a dense shaping term to the bonus.
Train with a much larger learning rate.
questions.explanation: A sparse reward rarely fires by chance at first. A dense term gives signal every step. The procedure warns against tweaking architecture before checking the reward.

questions.prompt: One reward term ranges 0–1 and another 0–1000. What goes wrong?
options: The larger term dominates, whatever the weights.
The policy stops training until both terms match.
Nothing, since the network learns the right scale itself.
The smaller term dominates, since it changes faster.
questions.explanation: Scale mismatches swamp the intended weighting. Normalise term scales before combining them.

questions.prompt: How is a behaviour-cloning policy trained?
options: Regression on (state, expert action) pairs
Self-supervised prediction of future frames
Trial and error against a reward function
Preference comparisons between two rollouts
questions.explanation: Listing 63.3 fits an MLP with MSE loss to expert actions. No reward and no exploration are involved.

questions.prompt: The tutorial collected 4,400 (state, action) pairs from 80 demonstrations. How many pairs per demonstration is that?
questions.explanation: 4,400 / 80 = 55 pairs per demonstration, one per control step.

questions.prompt: Why does the scripted expert work correctly at states it has never seen?
options: It uses a larger neural network.
It is a formula of state, not a fit to data.
It memorised every possible starting state.
It was trained on many more demonstrations.
questions.explanation: A PD controller with obstacle repulsion is defined everywhere. A cloned policy only knows the states it was shown.

questions.prompt: What does DAgger add to behaviour cloning?
options: A reward function to replace the demonstrations
A larger network trained for more epochs
More expert demonstrations from the original starting region
Expert labels for states the policy visits
questions.explanation: DAgger rolls out the trained policy, asks the expert what to do in the states it drifts into, adds them, and retrains. More demos from the same region miss those states.

questions.prompt: What kind of expert does DAgger need?
options: A reward model trained on human preferences
One that can be queried at arbitrary states
A fixed set of pre-recorded trajectories
A larger copy of the policy being trained
questions.explanation: A scripted controller, a human in the loop or a planner will do. Recorded trajectories can't label new states.

questions.prompt: A team runs one DAgger iteration and declares distribution shift solved. What's wrong?
options: Shift shrinks over rounds. It doesn't vanish.
One iteration is always enough, so nothing is wrong.
DAgger makes shift worse after the first iteration.
DAgger only works with a reward function added.
questions.explanation: The chapter calls this a common mistake. Each round finds new states the policy drifts into.

questions.prompt: Why is fine-tuning a pretrained VLA often the best starting point?
options: Broad skills mean little task data is needed.
It needs no task data at all.
It can't inherit biases from pretraining.
It runs faster at inference than a small from-scratch policy.
questions.explanation: The catch is inherited biases and much higher inference cost than a small network.

refLinks.label: §63.2.3 Route 3: Fine-Tuning a Pretrained VLA Policy

questions.prompt: The control loop has a very tight latency budget. Which route does the chapter's table point to?
options: Any route, since latency doesn't affect the choice
RL or imitation learning with a small, fast network
Fine-tuning a multi-billion-parameter VLA
Whichever route has the most training data
questions.explanation: A large VLA may not fit a tight loop. Small networks trained by RL or imitation do.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter call confident failure worse than obvious failure?
options: Confident policies always crash into obstacles.
It acts as smoothly when wrong, so nothing warns.
Obvious failures can't occur in simulation.
Confident failures happen more often than obvious ones.
questions.explanation: The policy doesn't hesitate outside its known region. Systems built on imitation need DAgger, an out-of-distribution detector, or a safety layer.

questions.prompt: Why did the demonstrations never teach obstacle avoidance?
options: The policy was trained for too few epochs.
The expert had no avoidance term.
The obstacle was removed while collecting demos.
No training path came within 1.2 units of it.
questions.explanation: Starts near the origin led straight to the target, never near the obstacle, so avoidance never appeared in the data. The check printed False.

questions.prompt: In distribution the cloned policy scored 40/40. Starting beside the obstacle it scored 0/40, while the expert scored 40/40. What does this show?
options: It fails off-distribution, which in-distribution tests hide.
The policy needed a larger network to reach the target.
Starting beside the obstacle makes the task impossible.
The expert had an unfair advantage from extra sensors.
questions.explanation: The expert succeeded from the same starts, so the task was possible. Procedure 63.4 says to test outside the distribution, because in-distribution results look finished.

bookExercises.prompt: Name the three practical routes to a working policy covered in this chapter, and for each, state whether it needs a reward function, demonstrations, or neither.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Reinforcement learning needs a reward function and no demonstrations. Imitation learning / behaviour cloning needs demonstrations and no reward function. VLA fine-tuning needs a small amount of task-specific data (demonstrations, or preference data) and can optionally combine with either a reward function or plain imitation.

bookExercises.prompt: Explain in one or two sentences why the behaviour-cloned policy in this chapter's Worked Example failed *confidently* rather than cautiously when tested out-of-distribution.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A neural network always outputs *something* for any input, whether or not that input resembles anything it was trained on. There's no built-in mechanism for it to recognise "this state is unlike anything I've seen" and respond with hesitation or a refusal. The cloned policy was fit only to states near the origin, so outside that region it's extrapolating with no signal telling it the extrapolation is unreliable, and it outputs a confident (and wrong) action exactly as smoothly as it outputs a confident (and right) one in-distribution.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 63.4's pattern, explain what it would mean if the printed check had shown `True` instead of `False`, and why the chapter insists on checking this before running the out-of-distribution test.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A `True` result would mean the demonstrations themselves had, at some point, come within the 1.2-unit obstacle-avoidance trigger radius, i.e. the expert's obstacle-repulsion behaviour actually fired during at least one demonstration, leaking some avoidance signal into the training data. That would contaminate the distribution-shift test: the cloned policy might then perform better than expected out-of-distribution not because imitation learning generalises well, but because a sliver of avoidance behaviour was accidentally present in training after all. Checking for `False` first ensures the subsequent 0/40 result is a clean measurement of distribution shift, not an artifact of leaked training signal.

bookExercises.prompt: The Worked Example reports 40/40 in-distribution success and 0/40 out-of-distribution success for the cloned policy, against 40/40 for the expert at the same out-of-distribution states. Using the DAgger algorithm sketch in this chapter's Exposition, describe what the *first* DAgger iteration would add to the training set, and why it targets exactly the gap this result exposes.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The first DAgger iteration rolls out the *current* (already-trained, already-failing) behaviour-cloning policy from a range of starting states, including states near the obstacle where it currently fails, and records exactly the states it visits. It then queries the scripted expert (not the cloned policy) for the correct action at each of those visited states, and adds those (state, expert-action) pairs to the training set before retraining. This directly targets the 0/40 failure because the new corrections come from precisely the region the current policy gets wrong, its own drift, rather than from more demonstrations near the origin, which the policy already handles correctly and gains nothing further from.

bookExercises.prompt: A robotics team wants to skip demonstration collection entirely and train their pick-and-place policy purely with RL because "it's more general." Using this chapter's Trade-offs section, write the two or three sentences you'd say back, including one concrete cost of that choice.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: RL being "more general" than imitation learning isn't automatic. It only generalises across whatever distribution the training reward and environment actually cover, and it needs a correct, well-shaped reward function to get there, which is often harder to build than it looks. If you already have good demonstrations, skipping them for RL trades a cheap, sample-efficient path for many thousands of trial-and-error episodes and a reward-design problem with its own failure modes (reward hacking, sparse-reward stalling). Concrete cost: reward mis-specification can produce a policy that scores well but does something visibly wrong, and that failure is often harder to diagnose than a demonstration-coverage gap.

bookExercises.prompt: An RL training run's reward curve is climbing steadily, but a video of the trained policy shows a legged robot repeatedly falling forward instead of walking. Using Procedure 63.1, name the pitfall and the fix.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: This is reward hacking: the reward (forward velocity) is being maximised by a degenerate behaviour (repeated forward falls) that technically satisfies the metric without doing the intended task (walking). The fix is not tuning the learning rate or architecture. It's inspecting the trained policy's actual behaviour directly, not just watching the reward curve, and then tightening or adding reward terms to close the loophole (e.g. penalising loss of balance or excessive impact force alongside the velocity reward).

bookExercises.prompt: Read the Ross, Gordon & Bagnell DAgger paper's abstract and introduction. Compare its framing of "no-regret online learning" to this chapter's plainer description of DAgger, and summarise in a few sentences what the formal framing adds that the pseudocode alone doesn't convey.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only, no single answer. The "no-regret online learning" framing casts DAgger's guarantee formally: because each iteration retrains on an aggregated dataset that includes corrections at the *actual* states the current policy visits, the sequence of policies produced behaves like an online learner competing against the best fixed policy in hindsight, and standard no-regret bounds then give a guarantee on cumulative future performance rather than just an intuition that "it should help." The pseudocode conveys the mechanical fix; the formal framing explains why iterating it converges rather than just plausibly improving things, and gives a way to reason about how many iterations are enough.

bookExercises.prompt: A team has a VLA checkpoint pretrained on a broad range of household manipulation tasks and a small set of teleoperated demonstrations for one new task. Using the decision table in this chapter's Exposition, argue for Route 3 over training a policy from scratch.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A pretrained VLA checkpoint already carries broad visual and instruction-following competence from its internet-scale pretraining, so fine-tuning it on a small teleoperated dataset only needs to teach the new task's specifics, not general perception or language understanding from zero. Training a policy from scratch has none of that prior competence to draw on, so it would need a much larger demonstration set (or a fully-specified reward and many RL episodes) to reach comparable generalisation. Route 3 is the cheaper path precisely because the "do you need broad generalisation" and "can you afford a large model at inference" conditions both favour it here (a household-manipulation VLA implies broad generalisation is exactly the goal).
